core_classification.analysis: “Je t’aime” strongly avows a loving state and also forms part of an affective verbal outpouring. Cyrano explicitly frames his words as arriving spontaneously and being thrown forth without arrangement, while “j’étouffe” and “je n’en peux plus” present speech as a release of overwhelming feeling; this supplies independent support for E beyond mere passionate delivery. The declaration participates weakly in courtship, but it does not itself clearly undertake a commitment or obligation.
core_classification.ambiguity: The utterance advances a romantic relationship while Cyrano speaks under Christian’s identity, which gives some possible performative force; nevertheless, its dominant forces are avowal and expressive discharge.

utterance_status.description: A directly spoken declaration by Cyrano to Roxane, complicated by his speaking in the balcony scene under Christian’s identity and ostensibly on Christian’s behalf.

contextual_interpretation: The immediate language presents an unpolished overflow of Cyrano’s feelings: he will cast out whatever words come, “sans les mettre en bouquet,” and places “Je t’aime” amid claims of choking, madness, and being unable to endure more. In the wider dramatic situation, Roxane understands the voice as expressing Christian’s love, whereas Cyrano is voicing his own genuine and highly observant love through that assumed identity. This interpersonal deception affects attribution and courtship consequences but does not prevent the utterance from functioning as a sincere avowal and expressive release for Cyrano.

evidence.supports: The explicit declaration and surrounding first-person descriptions strongly support T; the representation of emotional pressure and release also supports E.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “Tous ceux… / Qui me viendront, je vais vous les jeter, en touffe, / Sans les mettre en bouquet”
evidence.supports: Cyrano describes casting out the words as they come rather than arranging them, positive evidence that their production functions as spontaneous expressive discharge rather than only an intense assertion.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “Ton nom est dans mon cœur comme dans un grelot… le grelot s’agite, et le nom sonne !”
evidence.supports: The image represents Roxane’s name as involuntarily sounding within him, reinforcing reflexive or affect-driven verbal expression while also elaborating the claimed loving state.

evidence.quotation_or_description: Cyrano recalls Roxane’s changed hairstyle on a specific date and describes her hair as a dazzling light that colors his subsequent vision.
evidence.supports: Detailed, sustained attention to Roxane supports interpretation of “Je t’aime” as a substantive avowal rather than an empty token.

evidence.quotation_or_description: In the play’s balcony scene, Cyrano speaks to Roxane while she takes the declarations to be Christian’s, allowing Cyrano to express his own love through Christian’s assumed role.
evidence.supports: Explains the divided attribution, the deceptive courtship setting, and the limited P support without treating those contextual complications as ontology failure.

evidence.supports: Grounds the use of work-level knowledge concerning Cyrano, Roxane, Christian, and the dramatic impersonation.

background_knowledge.contribution: Used to identify the excerpt as the balcony-scene declaration in which Cyrano speaks under Christian’s identity, clarifying who voices the words, whose feelings they express, and how Roxane understands them.

ontology_assessment.diagnosis: T and E naturally capture the utterance’s joint force as a sincere avowal and an explicitly represented overflow of affect; a small P score captures its participation in courtship. The assumed identity and split attribution are contextual complications rather than missing dimensions of core force.

notes: E is supported not simply by intensity or exclamatory language, but by the passage’s explicit metapragmatic presentation of words arriving unarranged and being cast forth under emotional pressure.
